patient.chief_complaint: Daughter noticed increased confusion and word-finding difficulty for 3 days
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. D. is a 57-year-old woman with HCV-related cirrhosis who achieved sustained virologic response 2 months ago with direct-acting antiviral therapy, presenting at her daughter's insistence with a 3-day history of increasing confusion, word-finding difficulty, and personality change. The daughter noted her mother had been more forgetful, had missed two medication doses this week, was having difficulty balancing her checkbook (which she typically manages perfectly), and had been sleeping 12-14 hours per day. The patient herself minimized symptoms. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. She denied hematemesis or melena. She denied changes in her methadone dose or missed doses. Review of systems was positive for mild abdominal discomfort over the prior week and constipation. Her last bowel movement was 4 days ago. She had been started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) one week ago by her primary care physician for a urinary tract infection — this medication is generally avoided in cirrhosis as it can precipitate HE. The precipitant in this case required careful consideration: (1) constipation, (2) TMP-SMX (antibiotic that alters gut flora reducing lactulose efficacy), and (3) mildly elevated TSH suggesting undertreated hypothyroidism — all contributing to moderate HE in a patient with otherwise compensated cirrhosis.

output.query: Hepatic encephalopathy after HCV SVR cirrhosis — does SVR eliminate HE risk

results.title: Risk of hepatic decompensation after SVR in HCV-related cirrhosis
results.summary: SVR significantly reduces but does not eliminate risk of hepatic decompensation including HE in patients with established cirrhosis. Cirrhosis may partially reverse (Child-Pugh improvement) but portal hypertension may persist. HE risk remains, particularly with additional precipitants (constipation, infection, drugs). Lifelong surveillance and HE prophylaxis may be needed in cirrhotic patients even after SVR.

output.summary: Published cohort data indicate that SVR significantly reduces but does not eliminate the risk of hepatic decompensation in patients with established cirrhosis. Decompensating events, including episodes of overt encephalopathy, continue to occur post-SVR, particularly when additional precipitants (constipation, infection, drugs) are present. Clinical correlation recommended.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.
Visual evoked potentials have no role in HE workup; no demyelinating process is on the differential.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Lactulose 30 mL TID-QID titrated to 2-4 soft stools/day — address the constipation precipitant directly.
Rifaximin 550 mg BID — restart if interrupted.
Adjust levothyroxine dose for elevated TSH after acute illness resolves and recheck in 6 weeks.
Counsel about avoiding TMP-SMX and other broad-spectrum antibiotics that disrupt gut flora when possible.
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not stop rifaximin out of concern for antibiotic interaction with TMP-SMX — rifaximin is non-absorbable and essential for HE control.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
SVR12 cures HCV but does not reverse established cirrhosis morphology or portal hypertension — patients remain at HE risk and require ongoing surveillance.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt the gut microbiome on which lactulose/rifaximin efficacy depends; this is an under-recognized HE precipitant.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismiss HE as 'liver disease is cured'.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: SVR cures HCV viremia but cirrhosis and portal hypertension persist; HE risk continues for years post-SVR.
Hypothyroidism contributes to cognitive slowing but does not produce asterixis or respond to lactulose; treat HE concurrently.
